## Company: ABS-CBN Corporation (ABS)
Sector: Services / Media
ABS-CBN Corporation (ABS), originally incorporated as Bolinao Electronics Corporation on July 11, 1946, is a media and entertainment organization in the Philippines. The Company creates and produces entertainment and news and distributes its programs on different platforms such as cable and satellite TV (domestic and international), domestic free TV through various partnerships with local broadcasters, third-party digital platforms, its own streaming service iWantTFC, and co-production and syndication agreements with international streaming platforms.

The Company produces and co-produces feature films, television series and shows, concerts and events, music and podcasts, and digital video and audio features. ABS also manages and represents a stable of artists and talent, both on and off-camera.

ABS also programs and manages a lineup of cable and satellite channels for domestic and international platforms. Its international flagship channel, The Filipino Channel (TFC), distributes content to nearly 200 countries worldwide. The Company's digital assets include the domestic OTT platform iWantTFC, social media accounts for entertainment and news, and ABS-CBN.com, a Philippine information and entertainment website.

Source: The Company (2023) / SEC Form 17-A (2024)

thesis:
ABS-CBN produces and distributes entertainment, news and sports content across cable/satellite, its international TFC channel, and the iWantTFC streaming app, plus an artist-management arm. The business itself is easy enough to grasp — content, distribution, ad sales — well within a generalist's circle of competence. But understanding what it does isn't the same as understanding what it will look like as an investment: since Congress denied its broadcast franchise renewal in 2020, its core free-TV distribution model was gutted, and the company has been restructuring around cable, digital and content-licensing revenue ever since, with results that are still unstable (revenue up ~8.4%/yr on average over the last decade, ROIC averaging -17%).

There is no durable moat left to speak of. TFC and the talent roster give it some residual brand value in the Filipino diaspora content market, but its structural advantage — free-to-air broadcast reach — is gone and not coming back absent new legislation, which is a political variable, not a business one. Streaming and cable are commodity-competitive against GMA, TV5, and global platforms, and the company's own numbers (negative ROIC, shrinking book value at -14.6%/yr) show it hasn't found a profitable substitute business model yet. FCF growth of 108.6% looks impressive in isolation but is coming off a badly depressed base and says nothing about sustainable earning power.

Management quality is the biggest red flag here, not a mitigating factor. Recent disclosures show a board-level shutdown proposal floated amid an active Lopez family lawsuit (Federico Lopez ousted as Lopez Inc. president, suing his cousins), majority directors publicly rebutting "false claims," and repeated "clarification of news reports" filings — all signs of a company where family governance disputes are spilling into operational decisions. The ₱6B equity raise (I&C Holdings taking 27%, Lopez family diluted from 78% to 44%) is being sold as a balance-sheet fix, but it's dilutive recapitalization to plug losses and pay down debt, not growth capital, and it hands meaningful control to a new outside investor whose strategic intent for the network is untested.

On valuation, the 0.3x P/B and 21% dividend yield look like classic value-trap bait — no sticker price is computable because there's no reliable earnings base (P/E is N/A), and the "dividend yield" almost certainly reflects a stale/special payout rather than a sustainable cash return given the company posted losses and is raising dilutive equity to survive. Cheap on book value means little when book value itself is shrinking ~15%/yr and the equity is being diluted further. There's no margin of safety to calculate because there's no reliable intrinsic value to anchor to.

Bottom line: pass. No moat, negative returns on capital, family governance dysfunction spilling into board decisions, and an equity raise that dilutes existing holders to fund past losses — this fails Meaning, Moat, and Management, and Margin of Safety is unknowable rather than favorable. Revisit only if the franchise/legislative picture changes materially or if post-recapitalization financials show two-plus consecutive years of positive ROIC and stabilized revenue — neither is close to true today.
